column5: Two threads each grab a different lock first, which is precisely why the deadlock only shows up under sustained load. The fix is small and local: every thread must wait for the same primary lock before touching either resource, so the acquisition order becomes identical everywhere and no circular wait can form. Because the patch only moves two locking calls and touches no business logic, it is easy to review and safe to ship, and it removes the whole class of circular-wait deadlocks at once rather than papering over the symptom.

Legal needs two more working days to finish reviewing the vendor contract clause by clause, and procurement will not release the purchase order until the counterparty signs and returns it. So the two steps simply have to run in sequence, and there is no point in rushing them. What we can do right now is calmly wait for that countersigned copy to arrive, and once it does, start the integration work in the same sprint. This arrangement does not disturb any date we have already committed to, and it keeps the risk at a minimum because the commercial terms will be fixed before any code is written.

The thread pool runs dry because every incoming request blocks on a call to a slow downstream service and holds its thread for the whole duration. The workers just wait for the socket to come back, so the moment the downstream slows down, the entire pool stalls behind it and the callers upstream begin to time out as well, in a cascade that is hard to stop once it starts. The visible symptom looks like a pool that is too small, but the real cause is that each request occupies its connection for far too long. A short-term mitigation is to set a firm timeout on the downstream call so it cannot wait forever.

In summary, the migration reduced latency by roughly forty percent and cut the error rate almost in half, and every core metric moved in the right direction while no data was lost during the cutover. On the strength of that evidence the team should continue into the next phase exactly as planned, moving over the remaining tables at the same pace, without slowing down for a few unimportant fluctuations in secondary metrics. So far nothing in the data suggests that we need to change course, and the original judgement about the direction still holds, so we can keep going with confidence.

To recap what we covered today: a graph is just a set of nodes plus the edges that connect them, traversal is really about choosing the order in which you visit those nodes, and the difference between depth-first and breadth-first is mostly a matter of which tool fits which shape of problem, the former for exploring and backtracking, the latter for finding shortest paths. If those points are clear to you, then the exercise set that follows is well within your reach, and you can work through it on your own first before checking the answers.

To wrap up: this module is well covered by tests, the edge cases have mostly been considered, the naming is consistent with the rest of the project, and the error handling deals with the failures that actually happen rather than piling up unreachable branches. I did not find any substantial problems during review, so I recommend merging it as it stands and moving on to the next ticket on the board. There is no need to keep polishing it further, since that would only slow the overall delivery and make the sprint commitments slip again.
